name: Speech Rate Pattern Analysis
description: Analyzes speech rate patterns including pauses, syllable timing, and prosodic rhythm for voice cloning detection.
algorithm: Prosodic Rhythm and Speech Rate Forensics
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated or cloned speech by analyzing temporal speech patterns — the rhythm, timing, and rate variations that reflect cognitive and physiological speech production processes:

1. **Syllable Segmentation and Rate Computation**: The method segments the audio into syllable nuclei using a sonority envelope approach — computing the smoothed amplitude envelope of the signal (filtered in the 2–10 Hz modulation band, which corresponds to syllable rate) and detecting peaks as syllable centers. From this segmentation, the method computes: (a) local speech rate — syllables per second in a 2-second sliding window (typical range: 3–7 syllables/sec for conversational English), (b) articulation rate — syllables per second excluding pauses (typically 4–8 syl/sec), (c) pause duration distribution — the histogram of silent intervals, which in natural speech follows a log-normal distribution with mode ~200 ms for breath pauses and ~500 ms for cognitive planning pauses. AI-generated speech often shows unnaturally regular syllable timing with speech rate coefficient of variation < 0.08 (natural speech: 0.12–0.25).

2. **Prosodic Rhythm Metrics**: Natural speech exhibits characteristic rhythmic patterns that differ systematically across languages (stress-timed vs. syllable-timed vs. mora-timed). The method computes three standard rhythm metrics: (a) %V — the proportion of vocalic intervals in total speech time (English: ~40–45%), (b) ΔC — the standard deviation of consonantal interval durations (higher for stress-timed languages), (c) rPVI — the raw Pairwise Variability Index, measuring the average difference in duration between successive vocalic intervals. These metrics are computed from a forced alignment of the speech with its phonemic transcription (using Montreal Forced Aligner). AI-synthesized speech often shows rhythm metrics outside the natural range — typically too regular (%V variance too low) because TTS systems generate each phoneme duration from statistical models that don't capture the full variability.

3. **Hesitation and Disfluency Analysis**: Natural speech contains cognitive disfluencies — filled pauses (um, uh), false starts, word repetitions, and self-corrections — that follow predictable patterns related to cognitive load. The method detects and analyzes: (a) filled pause rate — typically 1–5 per 100 words in spontaneous speech, nearly zero in AI-generated speech, (b) filled pause placement — 'um' tends to precede difficult or infrequent words, 'uh' occurs at phrase boundaries, (c) self-correction patterns — real speakers correct errors within 1–3 words with characteristic repair prosody (rising pitch on the correction), (d) breathing patterns — natural speakers breathe approximately every 5–8 seconds, creating inter-breath-group pauses. The absence of disfluencies is paradoxically a strong indicator of AI generation, as current TTS systems produce unnaturally fluent speech.

4. **Long-Range Rate Adaptation**: Over longer speech segments (> 30 seconds), natural speakers exhibit systematic rate adaptation: (a) gradual warm-up — speech rate increases during the first 10–15 seconds as the speaker settles into a rhythm, (b) emphasis deceleration — speakers slow down for important points (rate drops 15–25% for emphasized segments), (c) list acceleration — items in a list are produced with progressively increasing rate, (d) fatigue effects — in long recordings, speech rate gradually decreases and pause duration increases. The method models these long-range patterns using a locally-weighted regression on the speech rate time series and checks for expected adaptation patterns. AI-generated speech typically maintains a constant or randomly varying rate without these systematic patterns.
parameters:
Syllable detection: sonority envelope, 2–10 Hz modulation band
Speech rate range: 3–7 syllables/sec (conversational)
Rate CV (natural): 0.12–0.25
Pause distribution: log-normal, mode ~200 ms (breath), ~500 ms (planning)
Forced alignment: Montreal Forced Aligner
Rhythm metrics: %V, ΔC, rPVI
%V range (English): 40–45%
Filled pause rate: 1–5 per 100 words
Breathing interval: 5–8 seconds
Warm-up detection window: first 15 seconds
accuracy: 79–88% accuracy detecting AI-generated speech via prosodic analysis. Disfluency absence detection achieves AUC of 0.86. Rhythm metrics provide F1-score of 0.84. Long-range rate adaptation adds 4–6% improvement for recordings > 30 seconds. Performance is best for spontaneous speech — read speech from scripts has naturally lower variability.
source: Grabe, E. & Low, E. L. (2002). Durational Variability in Speech and the Rhythm Class Hypothesis. Laboratory Phonology, 7, 515–546.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated speech through prosodic rhythm violations. Voice cloning detection in phone fraud investigations. Authenticating audio recordings of spontaneous speech. Distinguishing human narration from TTS-generated audio.
strengths:
• Exploits fundamental differences between planned and spontaneous speech production
• Disfluency analysis is paradoxically strong — AI speech is 'too perfect'
• Language-specific rhythm metrics provide cross-linguistic applicability
• Long-range patterns capture speech production dynamics TTS can't model
• Works independently of voice identity or speaker accent
limitations:
• Read speech from scripts has lower prosodic variability (closer to AI patterns)
• Short segments (< 5 seconds) provide insufficient rhythm analysis
• Some advanced TTS systems can now produce filled pauses
• Speaker variability — some individuals have naturally regular rhythm
• Background noise degrades syllable segmentation accuracy
